name: Spicy
baseline: binpac (Zeek's earlier protocol parser generator); not hand-written parsers
workload: Microbenchmarks of generated parsers (BytesLength, BytesUntil, WithUnit, WithUnitSwitch, Regex test cases) run inside Zeek, Spicy 1.16 / Zeek 8.2 versus binpac, reported in Gbps; plus an end-to-end Zeek run comparing Spicy versions.
claimed_speedup: Mixed. Per the zeek.org post as quoted in search snippets: WithUnit Spicy 9.357 Gbps vs binpac 4.663 Gbps (about 2.0x, derived from page data); WithUnitSwitch Spicy 11.061 vs binpac 4.866 Gbps (about 2.3x, derived from page data); Regex Spicy 4.197 Gbps vs binpac 0.000; BytesLength 0.003 vs 0.002 Gbps. BytesUntil goes the other way: binpac 2.316 Gbps vs Spicy 0.268 Gbps (Spicy about 8.6x slower, derived from page data). Version-over-version: Spicy 1.16 (Zeek 8.2) ran end-to-end in 1.339 s vs 1.430 s for Spicy 1.13 (Zeek 7.2), and 660 ms vs 758 ms spent in Spicy parsing.
stars_or_usage: 303 stars; the parser framework bundled with Zeek
tradeoffs: Spicy is a domain-specific language that compiles grammars to C++ (JIT or ahead of time) with incremental parsing of streams of arbitrary size and many built-in features; per the Zeek author it is slower than binpac in most real analyzers because binpac is barebones and often needs hand-written C++. Spicy is a code generator, not a drop-in for hand-written C++ parsers.
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: zeek.org, community.zeek.org and docs.zeek.org were egress-blocked in this session, so the post was never opened; every number above comes from WebSearch result summaries of the 2026-07 post (two separate searches returned consistent figures). Compiler, flags and CPU model are not known from what I could see, so tier C at best. The listed baseline guess (hand-written parsers) is wrong: the only numeric comparison found is against binpac. The result is mixed (Spicy loses BytesUntil by about 8x) and the post's own framing is that real analyzers see only a modest effect and Spicy stays slower in most of them. The spicy repo README and the GitHub wiki page on profiling carry no comparative numbers. Verifier should reopen the post from an environment that can reach zeek.org.

name: SRELL
workload: Matcheroni author's regex shootout (examples/regex/regex_benchmark.cpp, formerly matcheroni/benchmark.cpp): count matches of the Email, URI and IPv4 patterns from mariomka/regex-benchmark over its input-text.txt (a concatenation of the Learn X in Y minutes docs), also recording build time and binary size.
claimed_speedup: Snippet figures from the author's results sheet, -O3: SRELL 0.0174093 vs std::regex 0.724126 (about 41x, derived from page data; unit not visible, probably seconds); SRELL 'minimized' build 0.018889; Boost 0.084939; CTRE 0.061135; Matcheroni 0.057985. A second snippet of what looks like per-pattern msec values showed SRELL Email 0.018666 vs std::regex 0.001538 (SRELL slower), URL 0.000253 vs 0.000294, IP4 0.000336 vs 0.000362. The Matcheroni README of mid-2023 says 'SRELL is the performance champion' and 'std::regex is terrible by all metrics'.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 (a search summary said GCC 14; not confirmed from an opened page)
stars_or_usage: packaged in FreeBSD ports (devel/srell) and Debian-style distributions per search snippets; no GitHub repo
tradeoffs: Header-only template library with the std::regex class design but an ECMAScript-compatible engine with native Unicode (char8_t/char16_t/char32_t). By default it adds a lot to build time and binary size (the same README says so); a 'minimized' mode shrinks the binary but is still slow to build. ECMAScript semantics, not the std::regex default grammar, so patterns can differ.
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: akenotsuki.com, docs.google.com, linux.org.ru and the FreeBSD review pages were egress-blocked, so the results sheet was never opened; the numbers come from WebSearch summaries (two searches returned the same 0.0174093 / 0.724126 figures, but a third summary quoted per-pattern values in which SRELL is slower than std::regex on the Email pattern, so units and the exact run are unresolved). The numbers come from a competitor's (Matcheroni) README, whose harness is public at https://github.com/aappleby/Matcheroni/blob/main/examples/regex/regex_benchmark.cpp (SRELL case commented out by default) but whose result sheet states no CPU model; the opened early README (commit 53d152f) carries only the qualitative ranking, not numbers. Baseline stdlib (libstdc++ vs libc++) is unstated. License and 'active' status come from the awesome-cpp tag (BSD) and search snippets (release 4.069 with Unicode 17.0), not from an opened SRELL page. Verifier should reopen the sheet from an environment with access.

name: vcflib (vcfputtogetheragain)
baseline: vcfcreatemulti zig implementation (vcflib's own earlier tool for merging overlapping VCF records)
workload: Merging overlapping records back into multi-allelic VCF records on large VCF files (the companion step to vcfwave); the 13.8 MB scaffold612 sample is the only large input named in the commit.
claimed_speedup: ~200x faster on large VCFs (release notes wording)
stars_or_usage: 686 stars; packaged in Guix, Homebrew, Debian and Conda
tradeoffs: vcfputtogetheragain is plain C, with no C++ or zig dependency, and passes non-overlapping records through verbatim. Its --norm-multiallelic option deliberately differs from the zig semantics (keeps all ALT alleles, mirrors bcftools norm -m-), so outputs are identical to the zig tool only on shared inputs without that flag. vcflib as a whole is a collection of VCF tools, not a general CSV or VCF parsing library.
caveats: Weak entry. The only number is a single release-notes phrase ('~200x faster on large VCFs'); the commit that added the tool states no timings, input size, hardware or compiler flags. The baseline is vcflib's own zig implementation, which is not a widely used incumbent, so this is an internal before/after comparison and not a win over bcftools, htslib or vcftools. The listed baseline guess ('standard parser') has no numbers anywhere reachable: the README and docs carry none, and the 2022 PLoS Comput Biol paper (Garrison et al.), which may hold benchmarks, was egress-blocked here (journals.plos.org, PMC, Europe PMC, bioRxiv). A second in-repo figure (vcf-std validation from about 0.11 s to about 0.04 s on a 13.8 MB, 21k-record, 47-sample file) compares the tool with its own earlier code, so it is not a baseline win either. Verifier should check the paper before keeping or demoting.
